name: Community Acquired Pneumonia (non-severe)

pathogens.why: Outpatient/ward-level CAP without severity criteria is overwhelmingly community-acquired and typical-organism predominant. S. pneumoniae remains the leading cause across age groups; H. influenzae is more frequent in smokers and COPD. Atypicals (Mycoplasma, Chlamydophila) are added because clinical and radiographic findings cannot reliably distinguish typical from atypical pneumonia.

clinicalPearls: Typical and atypical pathogens cannot be reliably separated on clinical or radiographic grounds because both can produce overlapping syndromes; atypicals (Mycoplasma, Chlamydia, Legionella) are not seen on Gram stain or grown on standard media and are intrinsically resistant to beta-lactams (Harrison 22e p.1067).

In more than half of CAP cases no specific pathogen is identified despite history, examination, and imaging; in one large emergency-department series an etiology was established in under 8% (Harrison 22e p.1068).

Physical examination has limited diagnostic accuracy in pneumonia (sensitivity ~58%, specificity ~67%), so a compatible clinical picture plus a new infiltrate on chest film remains the diagnostic standard (Harrison 22e p.1068).
In the elderly the presentation may be subtle, manifesting as new or worsening confusion or decompensation of a chronic illness with few classic respiratory findings (Harrison 22e p.1068).
Gross hemoptysis raises concern for necrotizing pneumonia, such as that caused by community-associated MRSA (Harrison 22e p.1067).
Up to about 20% of patients have gastrointestinal symptoms (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea) in addition to constitutional and pulmonary findings (Harrison 22e p.1067-1068).

Aspiration pneumonia sits on a continuum with CAP/HAP and accounts for roughly 5-15% of CAP cases; modern organisms mirror the usual CAP/HAP flora, with anaerobes mainly relevant in poor dentition, lung abscess, necrotizing pneumonia, or empyema (Harrison 22e p.1066-1067).

Epidemiologic exposures can flag specific organisms (e.g. birds for Chlamydia psittaci/Histoplasma, recent hotel or cruise stay for Legionella, local influenza activity for influenza/pneumococcus/S. aureus) (Harrison 22e p.1067).

CAP can be complicated by cardiovascular events (heart failure, arrhythmia, myocardial infarction, stroke), especially in the elderly with pneumococcal or influenza pneumonia, attributed to increased myocardial load and inflammation-driven plaque destabilization, and these events may occur acutely or up to a year later (Harrison 22e p.1072).
harrison.pathophysiology: Pneumonia results from proliferation of microbial pathogens in the alveoli together with the host inflammatory response. Organisms reach the lower respiratory tract chiefly by microaspiration of oropharyngeal flora, but also by inhalation and direct mucosal spread; mechanical defenses (nasal hairs/turbinates, branching airways, mucociliary clearance, gag and cough reflexes) are imperfect barriers. Rather than simple invasion of a sterile space, current models view pneumonia as an emergent disturbance of the lung microbiota driven by self-reinforcing positive-feedback loops: an inciting epithelial/endothelial injury (often a viral infection plus microaspiration) releases cytokines, chemokines, and catecholamines that can selectively favor growth of organisms such as S. pneumoniae and P. aeruginosa, amplifying inflammation. When innate and adaptive immunity fail to contain this, mediators (IL-6 and TNF cause fever; IL-8 and G-CSF recruit neutrophils) drive an alveolar-capillary leak producing hypoxemia and radiographic infiltrates. Bacterial toxins amplify inflammation, and some pathogens blunt hypoxic vasoconstriction, worsening hypoxemia; reduced compliance, increased secretions, raised respiratory drive, and intrapulmonary shunting cause dyspnea and, when severe, respiratory failure (Harrison 22e p.1066). Pathologically, classic (lobar pneumococcal) pneumonia passes through edema, red hepatization, gray hepatization, and resolution; a bronchopneumonia pattern predominates in nosocomial disease while a lobar pattern is more typical of bacterial CAP, and viral pneumonias are alveolar rather than interstitial processes (Harrison 22e p.1066).
additionalDifferentials: Acute exacerbation of chronic bronchitis/COPD (Harrison 22e p.1068)
Tuberculosis (suggested by an upper-lobe cavitating lesion) (Harrison 22e p.1068)
nonInfectiousMimics: Heart failure / pulmonary edema (Harrison 22e p.1068, p.1072)
Pulmonary embolism / pulmonary infarction (Harrison 22e p.1068, p.1072)
Lung carcinoma (consider with relapse or recurrence in the same segment, raising concern for underlying neoplasm) (Harrison 22e p.1072)
Connective tissue disease involving the lungs (Harrison 22e p.1072)
additionalInvestigations: Sputum Gram stain and culture (recommended chiefly for hospitalized patients, particularly severe cases or those at risk for MRSA or P. aeruginosa; an adequate specimen needs >25 neutrophils and <10 squamous epithelial cells per low-power field) (Harrison 22e p.1068)

Blood cultures (reserved for high-risk patients such as neutropenia, asplenia, complement deficiency, chronic liver disease, or severe CAP, and those at risk for MRSA/P. aeruginosa; yield only ~5-14% in hospitalized CAP) (Harrison 22e p.1068)
Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigen tests (reserved for severe cases or relevant epidemiology; Legionella test detects only serogroup 1) (Harrison 22e p.1068)

Multiplex respiratory PCR / nasopharyngeal swab PCR (standard for viral diagnosis including influenza and coronaviruses; can also detect Legionella, M. pneumoniae, C. pneumoniae, mycobacteria) (Harrison 22e p.1068)

Procalcitonin and C-reactive protein (adjuncts for stewardship only; PCT is not accurate enough to diagnose bacterial CAP or to withhold initial antibiotics, and CRP is even less sensitive) (Harrison 22e p.1068-1069)
CT chest (for suspected loculated effusion, cavitary disease, or postobstructive pneumonia from tumor or foreign body) (Harrison 22e p.1068)
Diagnostic pleural fluid sampling for a significant effusion (Harrison 22e p.1072)
Follow-up chest radiograph ~4-6 weeks after hospitalization (not routinely needed in well, nonsmoking outpatients whose symptoms resolve in 5-7 days) (Harrison 22e p.1072)
redFlags: Septic shock requiring vasopressors or respiratory failure requiring invasive mechanical ventilation (major severe-CAP criteria mandating direct ICU admission) (Harrison 22e p.1069)
Confusion or disorientation, including new or worsening confusion in the elderly (Harrison 22e p.1068-1069)
Hypotension requiring aggressive fluid resuscitation (Harrison 22e p.1069)
Gross hemoptysis suggesting necrotizing pneumonia (Harrison 22e p.1067)
Failure to improve by ~day 3 of therapy, prompting reassessment for resistant or unexpected pathogen, sequestered focus (abscess/empyema), or a noninfectious mimic (Harrison 22e p.1072)
harrison.prognosis: Outcome depends on age, comorbidities, and site of care. Young patients without comorbidity generally recover fully in about 2 weeks, whereas older patients or those with comorbid illness may take several weeks longer. Overall mortality is under 5% for outpatients but ranges from roughly 12% to 40% for hospitalized patients depending on the patient category and the timeliness of appropriate antibiotics; in older patients the 1-year mortality after CAP exceeds the 30-day mortality. Fever and leukocytosis typically resolve in 2-4 days in otherwise healthy patients, while chest radiographic clearance is slowest (4-12 weeks). About 18% of hospitalized CAP patients are readmitted within a month (Harrison 22e p.1067, p.1072).
pitfalls: Treating a macrolide as adequate empirical monotherapy where high-level pneumococcal macrolide resistance is prevalent risks treatment failure (Harrison 22e p.1069).

Relying on chest radiography or clinical features to determine etiology is unreliable; imaging often cannot distinguish CAP from other conditions and seldom yields a specific organism (Harrison 22e p.1068).
Using procalcitonin or CRP in isolation to decide on or withhold antibiotics is inappropriate, as neither is sufficiently accurate for diagnosing bacterial CAP (Harrison 22e p.1068-1069).
Neither PSI nor CURB-65 is designed to determine the need for ICU admission, so they should not be used for that purpose (Harrison 22e p.1069).
Delayed ICU transfer of a deteriorating ward patient is associated with higher mortality than initial ICU monitoring of equally ill patients (Harrison 22e p.1069).
Inability to expectorate sputum may reflect dehydration rather than absence of disease; rehydration can yield a productive sample and a more apparent infiltrate (Harrison 22e p.1068).
Pneumonia that relapses or recurs in the same lung segment should prompt evaluation for an underlying neoplasm or focal abnormality such as bronchiectasis (Harrison 22e p.1072).
harrison.severityClassification: Two validated tools guide the site-of-care decision. The Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI) is a prognostic model using 20 variables (age, comorbidities, abnormal exam and laboratory findings) that stratifies patients into five classes with rising mortality (class 1 ~0.1%, class 2 ~0.6%, class 3 ~2.8%, class 4 ~8.2%, class 5 ~29.2%); classes 1-2 are generally suitable for outpatient care and class 3 for an observation unit. CURB-65 scores one point each for Confusion, Urea >7 mmol/L, Respiratory rate >=30/min, low Blood pressure (systolic <=90 or diastolic <=60 mmHg), and age >=65: a score of 0 (30-day mortality ~1.5%) suggests outpatient treatment, 1-2 generally warrants admission (unless driven only by age >=65), and >=3 (mortality ~22%) may need ICU care. PSI is better validated and more discriminating but harder to compute. Severe CAP (Harrison/IDSA-ATS criteria) is defined by either major criterion (invasive mechanical ventilation for respiratory failure, or septic shock requiring vasopressors), mandating ICU admission; presence of at least 3 of 9 minor criteria (RR >=30/min; PaO2/FiO2 <=250; multilobar infiltrates; confusion/disorientation; uremia with BUN >=20 mg/dL; leukopenia <4000/uL; thrombocytopenia <100,000/uL; hypothermia <36 degrees C; hypotension needing aggressive fluids) warrants ICU or high-level monitoring. Independent of these scores, inability to maintain oral intake, concerns about compliance (e.g. cognitive impairment, homelessness), or room-air O2 saturation <92% are indications for hospitalization (Harrison 22e p.1069).
